info.title: KnoxCall Client Management API
info.description:
The KnoxCall Client Management API provides programmatic access to manage your API gateway
resources including routes, secrets, clients, environments, webhooks, and API keys.

## Authentication

All requests must include an OAuth 2.1 access token **or** a legacy API key. The
recommended path for new integrations is the first-party SDKs, which mint, cache, and
refresh OAuth tokens for you (start with `knoxcall login` on a developer machine, or
`KNOXCALL_CLIENT_ID` / `KNOXCALL_CLIENT_SECRET` in CI). You can authenticate using any of:

- **Authorization header (OAuth 2.1 bearer token — recommended)**: `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>`
- **Authorization header (legacy API key)**: `Authorization: Bearer tk_xxx_yyy`
- **x-api-key header (legacy API key)**: `x-api-key: tk_xxx_yyy`

OAuth 2.1 access tokens (`kc_` prefix) are minted at the root-host token endpoint
`https://api.knoxcall.com/oauth/token` (not under `/v1`) using the `client_credentials`
or `authorization_code` grant. See the `OAuth2` security scheme and the `/oauth/*`
endpoints. Some resources that are managed exclusively through OAuth reject API-key auth
with a `403 use_oauth` error.

Long-lived API keys remain fully supported. They come in three types:
- **Standard keys** (`tk_` prefix) are used on the production API (`api.knoxcall.com`).
- **Test keys** (`tk_` prefix, type=test) are used on the sandbox API (`sandbox.knoxcall.com`).
- **Enterprise Access Keys** (`AKE` prefix) follow the format `AKE[16chars]:[40chars]`.

Using a test key on the production API (or vice versa) will return a `403 wrong_key_type` error.

## Request IDs

Every response — success or error — includes an `X-Request-Id` response header (a UUID).
Its value is identical to the `request_id` field in the response body (`meta.request_id`
on success, `error.request_id` on error). Quote it when contacting support.

## API Versioning

The API is versioned on two axes:

- **Major version — the `/v1` path prefix.** Breaking changes ship under a new major
  (`/v2`). `/v1` never receives a breaking change.
- **Minor version — the `KnoxCall-Version` header (dated, `YYYY-MM-DD`).** Send
  `KnoxCall-Version: 2026-08-05` to pin the behaviour of a specific dated release. Omit
  the header to get the newest minor version. Every response echoes the resolved version
  back in a `KnoxCall-Version` response header.

Within a major version, **additive changes are not breaking** and may appear without a new
dated version: new endpoints, new optional request fields, new response fields, new
`error.type` values, and new enum members. Clients must tolerate unknown response fields
and unknown `error.type` values (see the `ErrorResponse` schema).

An **unknown or malformed** `KnoxCall-Version` value returns `400` with
`error.type: invalid_api_version`.

## Rate Limiting

API keys can have optional rate limits configured. When a limit is configured, the
following headers are emitted on **every** response (not only `429`s):
- `X-RateLimit-Limit` -- maximum requests allowed per window
- `X-RateLimit-Remaining` -- remaining requests in the current window
- `X-RateLimit-Reset` -- epoch seconds at which the window resets

When the limit is exceeded the API returns `429` (`rate_limit_exceeded` / `rate_limited`)
and additionally sets `Retry-After` (seconds until the window resets).

## DPoP sender-constrained tokens, and the server nonce

A token minted with a `cnf.jkt` binding (DPoP, RFC 9449) requires a `DPoP` proof header
on every request, signed over the request's method and canonical public URL.

**Every response to a request that carried a `DPoP` header also carries a
`DPoP-Nonce` response header** -- mints, refusals and successful calls alike, on
`POST /oauth/token`, `/v1`, the tenant data plane, the self-hosted proxy and the AI
gateway. The value is stateless and changes every minute; the server accepts the current
and the previous minute's, so a nonce is good for 60-120 seconds.

The header is issued because the REQUEST carried a proof, not because the token happened
to be bound. Two consequences a client can rely on: a request sending
`Authorization: DPoP` against a token with no `cnf` binding is refused and STILL carries
a `DPoP-Nonce`; and a plain `Bearer` request never carries the header at all, so its
absence is not a signal that the server stopped issuing nonces.

The rule is **verify-if-present**: a proof carrying a `nonce` claim must carry one the
server would issue now, or the request is refused; a proof carrying NO `nonce` is still
accepted. Sending one is therefore an optimisation, never a requirement.

When a nonce is required and the one presented is stale or absent-but-demanded, the two
RFC 9449 surfaces answer differently:

- `POST /oauth/token` (authorization server, RFC 9449 section 8.1) answers **400** with
  the OAuth error body `{"error": "use_dpop_nonce", "error_description": "..."}`.
- `/v1`, the tenant data plane, the self-hosted proxy and the AI gateway (resource
  server, section 8.2) answer **401** with `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP
  error="use_dpop_nonce"`. On `/v1` the envelope's `error.type` is `use_dpop_nonce` too;
  the tenant data plane keeps its deliberately opaque `Unauthorized` body, so on that
  surface the header is the only signal.

Both refusals carry a fresh `DPoP-Nonce`, so a client never needs an extra round trip to
learn the value. A stale nonce is refused BEFORE the proof's `jti` is claimed, so the
retry is not then refused for an unrelated reason -- re-sign once with the new nonce and
a new `jti`. Every official SDK does this for you.

## Idempotency

All mutating requests (`POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE`) accept an idempotency key so a
retried request is executed at most once. Supply it as `X-Idempotency-Key`
(the standard `Idempotency-Key` spelling is also accepted), max 255 characters.

- Replaying a completed request with the same key returns the original stored response,
  annotated with an `X-Idempotent-Replay: true` response header.
- A key that is still being processed returns `409 request_in_progress`.
- Re-using a key with a **different** request body returns `422 idempotency_key_reuse`.
- A malformed key returns `400 invalid_idempotency_key`.

## Pagination

List endpoints support pagination with the following query parameters:
- `page` -- page number (default: 1)
- `per_page` -- items per page (default: 20, max: 100)
- `sort` -- field to sort by (varies per endpoint)
- `order` -- sort direction: `asc` or `desc`

Paginated responses include a `meta` object with `total`, `page`, `per_page`, and `total_pages`.

### Offset ceiling

The server derives its SQL offset as `(page - 1) * per_page` and will not
exceed 100,000 rows, so `page` is clamped to `floor(100000 / per_page) + 1`
(1,001 at the maximum `per_page` of 100). Two consequences:

- `meta.page` echoes the **effective** page, which may be lower than the one
  you asked for. It always matches the rows returned.
- `meta.total_pages` is capped at that same page, so it is
  `min(ceil(total / per_page), floor(100000 / per_page) + 1)`. A pager that
  walks until `page >= total_pages` therefore terminates.

`meta.total` still reports the true row count. If `total` exceeds
`total_pages * per_page` you are being truncated by the ceiling -- narrow
the result set with a filter (date range, status, resource id) instead of
paging deeper.

## Error Handling

All errors follow one canonical shape everywhere on `/v1`:
`{"error": {"type", "message", "request_id"}}`. The `type` field is a machine-readable
category (see the `ErrorResponse` schema for the full enum). Request-body validation
failures are always `400 validation_error`; the one `422` case is `idempotency_key_reuse`.

post.description:
Start creating a KnoxCall account and tenant - no browser required.

This call **never returns a credential**. It always answers `202` with an opaque
`claim_handle` and emails a sign-in link to the address. The tenant is created when that
link is clicked; the caller then polls `POST /v1/signup/claim` with the handle to collect
a one-time **test API key** and the seeded Test-mode demo route, so the whole integration
can still be built headlessly against `sandbox.knoxcall.com`.

Only available on `api.knoxcall.com` (not the sandbox host). Rate limited to 3 signups
per hour per IP.

**Account existence is NOT observable on this endpoint.** Every response - accepted or
rejected - is independent of whether the address already has an account: same status,
same body shape, a handle drawn from the same generator with the same lifetime, and no
credential anywhere. An address that already has an account receives a sign-in link and a
handle that stays `pending` forever. (Before 2026-08-28 this endpoint answered `201` plus
an instant API key for a new address and `202` for a registered one, which was a complete
account-existence oracle; that contract is withdrawn.)

email.description: Account owner's email. Receives the sign-in link that creates the tenant.

full_name.description: Owner's full name. Defaults to the tenant name.

tenant_slug.description: Desired subdomain ({slug}.knoxcall.com): 3-40 chars of lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting and ending with a letter or digit. Reserved subdomains (www, api, admin, well-known brand names, ...) and the sandbox- prefix are rejected. Omit to have one derived from tenant_name automatically (recommended for headless callers - the server converges on an available slug on its own).

country.description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code. Used to derive the data region when region is omitted. Enforced: anything else (an alpha-3 code such as USA, or a country name) is a 400 invalid_request, not a deferred failure - the column is two characters wide.

region.description: Explicit data region. Immutable after signup.

202.description:
Accepted - the ONLY success status, returned identically whether or not the address
already has an account. Poll `claim_path` with `claim_handle` once the emailed
sign-in link has been clicked.

claim_handle.description: Opaque single-use handle (`sck_` plus 43 url-safe characters). Present on every accepted signup. Treat it as a secret: it is what collects the starter credential.

claim_path.description: Path to poll, on the same API host.

expires_at.description: After this, the handle is rejected exactly like an unknown one.

post.summary: Collect starter credentials for a signup claim
post.description:
Poll a `claim_handle` returned by `POST /v1/signup`.

Answers `202` (`status: pending`) until the emailed sign-in link has been clicked, then
`200` once with the tenant, the seeded Test-mode demo route and a one-time test API key.
The credential is minted at collection time and shown exactly once - a second poll gets
`409`.

Unauthenticated by design: the claim handle is the bearer. It is unguessable (256 bits),
single-use, and expires. An unknown handle and an expired one get the same `404`, and a
handle whose link has not been clicked polls `pending` regardless of whether the address
already had an account.

200.description: Ready. The starter api_key value is returned exactly once - store it before anything else.

starter.description: Seeded Test-mode demo route + one-time test API key.

api_key.description: Plaintext test key - shown only in this response.

curl.description: Ready-to-run curl that exercises the demo route.

202.description:
Not ready - the sign-in link has not been used yet. Identical for a claim whose link
is simply unclicked and for one raised against an address that already had an account.

get.description: Returns a paginated list of routes belonging to the authenticated account.

post.description:
Creates a new proxy route. The route name must be unique within your account.
The route will be created in the specified `base_environment` (defaults to `production`).

409.description:
Two refusals share this status; `error.type` tells them apart. `conflict` —
a route with this name or slug already exists in this tenant and data space.
`intercept_route_conflict` — `intercept_enabled: true` was requested and another
intercept-enabled route already covers the same upstream host and base path in the
base environment (only one route may take a host's traffic).

error.message: A route with this name already exists.
Route "hubspot-crm" already intercepts api.hubapi.com/crm/v3 in production. Turn Intercept off on that route first, or leave it off on this one.

get.description: Returns full details of a single route, including configured environment names.

patch.description:
Updates one or more fields on an existing route. Only provided fields are changed.

**A route that decrypts or detokenizes.** When the route carries a standing `decrypt` or
`detokenize` field action (`POST /routes/{routeId}/actions`, either direction), giving it
a NEW destination — a `target_base_url` or per-method `target_url` it does not already
store, or switching on one it stores but does not send to (`enabled: true` on a disabled
environment, an idle URL copied into the base URL) — sends the opened values to that host
on every later call, so it needs what
attaching the action needed: a token issued to a person (knoxcall login, a device or
authorization-code grant) is refused (`403 forbidden`); a machine credential must hold the
action's own permission (`transit:decrypt` on the action's key, `vaults:detokenize` on its
vault — `403 forbidden` from the key's policy, `403 insufficient_scope` for a narrowed
token). Re-sending a URL the route already stores, removing one, and every route without
such an action are unaffected. The change is recorded in the audit log
(`route.destination_change`) before it is written. Make it from the dashboard as an Owner
or Admin (a fresh second factor is asked) when no machine credential holds the permission.

409.description:
Two refusals share this status; `error.type` tells them apart. `request_in_progress` —
a request with the same idempotency key is still being processed: retry after a short delay without changing the body.
`intercept_route_conflict` — `intercept_enabled: true` was requested and another
intercept-enabled route already covers the same upstream host and base path in the
base environment (only one route may take a host's traffic).

error.message: A request with this idempotency key is still being processed.
Route "hubspot-crm" already intercepts api.hubapi.com/crm/v3 in production. Turn Intercept off on that route first, or leave it off on this one.

delete.description: Permanently deletes a route and all of its environment overrides.

get.description: Returns a paginated list of proxied request logs for the specified route, ordered by timestamp descending.

200.description: A paginated list of request logs.

get.description: Returns all environment-specific configuration overrides for a route.

put.description:
Creates or updates an environment-specific configuration override for a route.
The environment must already exist in your account. Fields not provided will retain
their existing values on update, or be null on initial creation.

**A route that decrypts or detokenizes.** When the route carries a standing `decrypt` or
`detokenize` field action (`POST /routes/{routeId}/actions`, either direction), giving it
a NEW destination — a `target_base_url` or per-method `target_url` it does not already
store, or switching on one it stores but does not send to (`enabled: true` on a disabled
environment, an idle URL copied into the base URL) — sends the opened values to that host
on every later call, so it needs what
attaching the action needed: a token issued to a person (knoxcall login, a device or
authorization-code grant) is refused (`403 forbidden`); a machine credential must hold the
action's own permission (`transit:decrypt` on the action's key, `vaults:detokenize` on its
vault — `403 forbidden` from the key's policy, `403 insufficient_scope` for a narrowed
token). Re-sending a URL the route already stores, removing one, and every route without
such an action are unaffected. The change is recorded in the audit log
(`route.destination_change`) before it is written. Make it from the dashboard as an Owner
or Admin (a fresh second factor is asked) when no machine credential holds the permission.

delete.description: Deletes an environment-specific configuration override, reverting the route to its base configuration for that environment.

get.description:
Returns the declarative field-level encrypt/decrypt/tokenize/detokenize
actions the proxy applies to this route, ordered for execution.

post.description:
Adds a field-level action to a route. On each proxied request (or
response), the selectors are matched against the payload and the
configured action is applied to the selected fields on the wire.
`tokenize` / `detokenize` actions require `key_name` (the vault name);
`encrypt` / `decrypt` default to the tenant's default transit key when
`key_name` is omitted.

**Scope depends on the `action` in the body.** A route action is a
STANDING grant: once stored, every request through the route runs it
unattended. So `action: detokenize` additionally requires
`vaults:detokenize` (or `vaults:*`) and `action: decrypt` additionally
requires `transit:decrypt` (or `transit:*`) on the access token's grant —
the same scopes the equivalent one-shot calls require. `encrypt` and
`tokenize` stay on `routes:write`: both close data and neither reads
anything back. A token narrowed to `routes:write` that asks for a
`detokenize` or `decrypt` action receives `403 insufficient_scope` and
nothing is written. API keys and key-mirrored clients carry no scope
grant and are unaffected. Changed 2026-09-12.

delete.description: Removes a field-level action from a route.

200.description: Route action deleted. `deleted` echoes the action ID.

get.description: Returns a paginated list of secret metadata. Secret values are never returned by the API.

post.description:
Creates a new encrypted secret. Pass `secret_type` to choose the secret variant:

| `secret_type` | Use case |
|---|---|
| `string` (default) | Any static value — API keys, tokens, passwords |
| `oauth2` | OAuth2 connection with automatic token refresh |
| `certificate` | TLS/mTLS certificate + optional private key |

For `oauth2` secrets, see the field reference under **POST /secrets/oauth2**.
For `certificate` secrets, see **POST /secrets/certificate**.
String secrets require only `name` and `value`.

get.description: Returns a paginated list of authorized clients.

post.description:
Creates a new authorized client. Clients represent users or servers that are
allowed to call your routes. The `ip_address` field supports individual IPs,
CIDR notation, and ranges.

get.description: Returns full details of a single client, including its route assignments.

patch.description: Updates one or more fields on an existing client. Only provided fields are changed.

delete.description: Permanently deletes a client and removes all of its route assignments.

get.description:
Returns all credentials attached to a client. Secret material
(HMAC secrets, private keys) is redacted from the `data` object.

post.description:
Attaches a credential to a client. Supported kinds in v1: `ip` and
`mtls_thumbprint`.

- `ip` — `data.value` must be an IP address or CIDR range.
- `mtls_thumbprint` — either register an existing certificate with
  `data.sha256_thumbprint` (64 hex chars), or set `data.mode` to
  `issue` to have KnoxCall mint a client certificate. For the issue
  mode the response carries a one-shot `reveal` object with the PEM
  bundle (certificate, private key, CA chain) — **it is returned
  exactly once and never stored**.

A token issued to a person (`knoxcall login`, a device or
authorization-code grant) cannot use `mode: issue` and gets **403
`forbidden`**, whatever the person's role: the response would carry a
private key. Register a certificate you generated yourself by its
`sha256_thumbprint`, issue it from the dashboard, or use an API key.

mtls_issue.summary: Mint a new mTLS client certificate

200.description:
The created credential. For `mtls_thumbprint` with `mode: issue`,
includes the one-shot `reveal` PEM bundle.

patch.description: Updates a credential's `enabled` flag and/or `label`. At least one field is required.

delete.description: Permanently removes a credential from a client.

get.description:
Returns all environments for the authenticated account, ordered with the default
environment first followed by creation date ascending.

post.description:
Creates a new environment. Environment names must contain only lowercase letters,
numbers, hyphens, and underscores. Multiple environments require a Pro or Enterprise plan.

patch.description: Updates one or more fields on an existing environment. Only provided fields are changed.

delete.description:
Permanently deletes an environment. The default environment cannot be deleted.
Environments that are in use by route configuration overrides cannot be deleted
until all overrides are removed first.

error.message: Cannot delete the default environment.

409.description: Environment is in use by route configurations.

error.message: Environment is in use by route configurations. Remove all route environment overrides first.

get.description:
Returns a paginated list of API keys. Keys are masked -- the full key value is
only returned at creation time and cannot be retrieved again.

Every row carries `expires_at`, and it is worth reading rather than assuming: a key
created without an explicit expiry choice is on a 90-day clock, and `null` is the
only value that means "never expires".

200.description: A paginated list of API keys.

post.description:
Creates a new API key. The full key value is included in the response and will
**never be shown again**. Store it securely immediately. The key type (standard or
test) is determined by which API host you create it on -- production creates standard
keys, sandbox creates test keys.

**Every key expires.** Choose a lifetime with at most one of `expires_in_days`,
`expires_at` or `never_expires`; send none of them and the key gets **90 days**.
The resolved instant comes back as `expires_at` on the response and on every later
read, and it is enforced on authentication — so a long-lived integration needs
either a rotation schedule or an explicit `never_expires: true`.

plain.summary: A key with no roles (default-denied on every policy-gated endpoint)

terraform.summary: A Terraform credential — assign the seeded `Key — Infrastructure` role

short_lived.summary: A 30-day key for a one-off migration

never_expires.summary: A key with no expiry — valid until revoked by hand

200.description: The created API key with the full key value.

400.description:
The request body failed validation (`validation_error`), or the expiry choice
could not be resolved.

`conflicting_expiry_fields` and `invalid_expiry` are specific to this endpoint:
they are NOT flattened into `validation_error`, because "you sent two of them"
and "the one you sent is out of range" need different fixes and a caller
automating key rotation has to tell them apart.

error.message: name is required.

conflicting_expiry_fields.summary: More than one expiry field sent

error.message: Send at most one of expires_in_days, expires_at or never_expires.

invalid_expiry.summary: The expiry is out of range, or in the past

error.message: expires_in_days must be an integer between 1 and 365.

403.description:
The privilege-escalation ceiling refused the request: a role in `role_ids`
grants a permission the calling key does not itself hold. The message names
the offending grant verbatim so it can be removed or matched. A key can never
mint a key more privileged than itself.

**A scope-narrowed OAuth token cannot mint a key at all**, with or without
`role_ids`, and also gets `403 privilege_escalation`. An API key carries no
scope narrowing (on the data plane it can invoke every route in its mode), so
any key such a token minted would exceed the token's own grant. Mint keys with
an API key, or with an OAuth token whose scope is not narrowed (no scope
requested, or `*`).

Also returned as ordinary `forbidden` when the calling key lacks
`api_key:create`.

privilege_escalation.summary: The requested role exceeds the caller's own grants

error.message: This API key cannot grant a permission it does not itself hold. Refused grant from role "Key — Infrastructure": {"resource_type":"vault","actions":["create","read","update","delete","tokenize","detokenize"],"effect":"allow"} — no rule in your own policy set grants it.
Permission denied: create on api_key — no matching rule (default deny)

404.description:
One or more `role_ids` do not exist in this tenant. Another tenant's role UUID
is indistinguishable from a nonexistent one, by design.

error.message: Role not found in this tenant: b3f1c2d4-5e6f-4a7b-8c9d-0e1f2a3b4c5d.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The API key UUID or key_id (e.g. `tk_abc`).

delete.description:
Revokes an API key, permanently disabling it. A revoked key cannot be reactivated.
You cannot revoke the key currently being used to authenticate this request.

400.description: Cannot revoke the currently-used API key.

error.message: Cannot revoke the API key currently in use.

get.description:
Returns the tenant's permission roles so a machine can discover the id to pass in
`role_ids` when creating an API key. Read-only: there is no create, update or
delete on `/v1`.

Only the SEEDED key roles (`seeded: true`) are accepted in `role_ids`. Custom
roles are being retired in favour of per-key permissions: none can be created,
and this list still returns any a tenant already has (`seeded: false`), which
`POST /v1/api-keys` refuses with `403 forbidden`. Filter on `seeded`.

The seeded machine roles (`applies_to: [api_key]`) are `Key — Invoke`,
`Key — Read-only`, `Key — Editor` and `Key — Infrastructure`. The last is the one
to attach to a Terraform or CI credential — it covers the whole provisioning
surface and deliberately excludes secret reveal, custody transitions,
workload-identity bindings and the ephemeral proxy.

Requires the `role:list` permission, which all four seeded machine roles carry.

parameters.name: subject_kind
parameters.description: Return only roles whose `applies_to` includes this audience. `api_key` also returns a tenant's existing custom key roles (`seeded: false`), which `role_ids` refuses; the roles assignable to a key are the `seeded: true` rows.

post.description: Creates a workflow from a graph definition. The definition is validated for structure (a reachable trigger, no cycles, no dangling edges) and for credential custody — a definition that stores a credential in cleartext is refused, because every member of the tenant can read a workflow definition; reference a Secret instead. Steps that are not yet complete are accepted, but the workflow is then created with `enabled: false` (check the `enabled` field of the response): an unpublishable definition is never the running one. Requires the workflow create scope.

422.description: The workflow definition was refused (`invalid_definition`) — the graph is structurally invalid (no trigger, a cycle, an edge to a node that does not exist), or the definition stores a credential in cleartext, which is refused on every write: move it to a Secret and reference that Secret from the step. A definition whose STEPS are merely incomplete is not refused; the workflow is created with `enabled: false` instead, and publishing it is what makes it live. Also returned when the idempotency key was reused with a different request (`idempotency_key_reuse`).

A workflow may never be LIVE with a definition that cannot be published, so `enabled: true` re-evaluates the STORED definition, and a definition that replaces the one on an already-enabled workflow must itself publish. Unlike create — which keeps your data and returns `enabled: false` — an update refuses (422) rather than switching a running workflow off. Requires the workflow update scope.

422.description: The workflow definition was refused (`invalid_definition`) — the graph is structurally invalid (no trigger, a cycle, an edge to a node that does not exist), or the definition stores a credential in cleartext, which is refused on every write: move it to a Secret and reference that Secret from the step. A definition whose STEPS are merely incomplete is not refused by that storage rule. The same status and the same `invalid_definition` type also answer the LIVE rule: `enabled: true` on a workflow whose stored definition could not be published, or a definition that introduces a publish blocker onto a workflow that is already enabled. The message names which of the two refused. Also returned when the idempotency key was reused with a different request (`idempotency_key_reuse`).

get.description:
A keyset-cursor feed of audit events, for pollers and SIEM shippers.

`GET /audit-logs` is offset-paginated over `created_at DESC`, which is
correct for a console and wrong for a feed: rows inserted while a poller
pages shift the offsets underneath it, so events are skipped or repeated
with no way to tell which. This endpoint is ordered by the monotonic
`seq` and resumes from an opaque cursor.

**Contract**
- **Ordering** — ascending `seq`, stable across calls.
- **Delivery** — AT LEAST ONCE. Dedupe on `id` (a uuid, stable per row).
- **Freshness** — trails real time by a short watermark, reported as
  `meta.watermark_seconds`, so a row cannot appear behind a cursor you
  have already passed.
- **Termination** — `next_cursor` is `null` when you have drained
  everything outside the watermark. That is not the end of the feed:
  poll again later with your last non-null cursor.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: The opaque `meta.next_cursor` from a previous response. Omit to start at the beginning.

parameters.name: action_prefix
parameters.description: Prefix-match on the action name — subscribe to a whole SURFACE rather than to one event. `ai_gateway.` is the entire AI Gateway surface (denials, agent and MCP-server creation, token mints, geo-velocity anomalies, canary leaks, unpriced models), INCLUDING action names added after your integration was built. Composes with `action` and `resource_type`. `_` and `%` are matched literally, not as wildcards.

200.description: A page of audit events, oldest first.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `cursor` on the next call. `null` means you have drained the feed to the watermark.

get.description:
A keyset-cursor feed of proxied API requests — the per-call log, as
opposed to `/audit-logs`, which records configuration CHANGES.

Ordered by the monotonic row id and resumed from an opaque cursor, for
the same reason the audit event feed is: offset pagination over a table
that is being written to skips and repeats rows with no way to tell
which.

**Contract**
- **Ordering** — ascending `cursor`, stable across calls.
- **Delivery** — AT LEAST ONCE. Dedupe on `request_id`.
- **Freshness** — trails real time by `meta.watermark_seconds`.
- **Termination** — `next_cursor` is `null` when you have drained
  everything outside the watermark. Poll again later with your last
  non-null cursor.

**What this endpoint does not return.** Captured request and response
BODIES are never on this surface at any permission level. They are
available only from the audited admin route, which gates them on
`log:read_payload`.

**Identity fields.** `src_ip`, `matched_client_id` and
`identification_method` require the `log:read_identity` permission. When
it is denied the fields are ABSENT from each row — not null — and
`meta._redacted` contains `identity`.

get.summary: Merkle inclusion proof for a request
get.description:
Returns cryptographic evidence that a request log entry existed, in the
form it is returned in, at the time it was anchored.

**How the anchoring works.** On a schedule, KnoxCall takes a contiguous
range of request log rows, hashes them into an RFC 6962-style Merkle
tree, and appends the root to its hash-chained critical audit log. That
chain is verified daily, so the root is evidence that is expensive to
alter after the fact. This endpoint hands you the
sibling hashes needed to walk your own row up to that root.

**Verify it yourself.** Recompute the leaf hash from the returned
`leaf_fields` using the scheme in `verification.note`, then fold in each
`proof` step (`right: true` means the sibling goes on the right) and
compare with `anchor.merkle_root`. `anchor.chain_row_hash` ties that root
to its row in the audit chain.

**Outcomes.** Always `200` when the request exists and is yours; read
`anchored` and `verified` rather than the status code.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `anchored: false`, `reason: not_yet_anchored` | Too recent. Retry later. |
| `verified: true` | `proof` is present and reaches the anchored root. |
| `verified: false`, `reason: range_incomplete` | Rows the anchor covered have since been deleted by retention, so the tree can no longer be recomputed and no proof can be produced. Expected on old entries; not a sign of tampering. |
| `verified: false`, `reason: range_grew` | The range now holds more rows than the anchor counted. What that means depends on how the anchor cut its range, and `detail` says which case applies. An anchor that sealed its range after every write in it had finished can only have gained a row by something other than ordinary traffic, either an insert that named its id or an id sequence that was set backwards: escalate, as for `root_mismatch`. An older anchor, one that records no cut rule, cut its range by timestamp and could leave a committed row out; it stays valid for the set it read, and the extra row is not covered by any anchor today. |
| `verified: false`, `reason: root_mismatch` | The range reproduces the anchor's leaf count but not its root — a row in it was ALTERED after anchoring. This is a tamper indication. Escalate. |

A proof is never returned alongside a failed verification.

**Retention caveat, stated plainly.** An anchor's tree spans every
tenant's rows in its range, so retention deletion — including another
customer's — can make a specific proof unreproducible. The anchor itself
is permanent and still attests the root it committed; what decays is the
ability to demonstrate membership in it.

200.description: The proof, or a named reason why one cannot be produced.

post.description:
Creates an OAuth 2.1 client. Confidential clients receive a
`client_secret` in the response — **it is shown exactly once and can
never be retrieved again** (public clients get `client_secret: null`).
`redirect_uris` are required when the `authorization_code` grant is
enabled and must use `https://` (or `http://localhost`).

`allowed_scopes` must narrow something: an empty list and a universal
entry (`*` or `*:*`) both mean "every scope" and are refused with `400`.

**Called with a scope-narrowed OAuth token**, the client you create must be
one that token could itself hold: every `allowed_scopes` entry must appear
verbatim in the token's own scope, and `grant_types` must be
`client_credentials` only (any other grant lets the client act as a
different principal). Otherwise the call returns `403 privilege_escalation`
and nothing is created.

patch.description:
Updates one or more fields. Only provided fields are changed. Grant
types cannot be changed after creation.

**`step_up_scopes` requires an explicit `oauth_client:step_up_manage`
policy grant**, which no seeded role carries and no wildcard (`*:*`)
rule satisfies. That field controls the re-authentication a HUMAN is
forced through at both consent surfaces - the authorize endpoint and
the device-activation page a CLI login uses - so a machine credential
may not weaken it casually; the `/admin` twin demands a fresh step-up
verification instead. A request whose body carries `step_up_scopes`
without the grant returns `403 forbidden` and changes nothing - including
the other fields in the same body. Every other field needs only
`oauth_client:update`.

**`active: false` is a containment action and it is permanent for the
tokens outstanding at that moment.** Disabling a client revokes every
access and refresh token it has issued, exactly as `DELETE
/v1/oauth-clients/{id}` does. Re-enabling the client with `active: true`
restores its ability to MINT new tokens; it does not bring the revoked
ones back. Send `active: false` only when you mean to end the credential,
not to pause it.

Setting `allowed_scopes` to a universal list (`*` or `*:*`) is refused
with `400` unless the client already holds one — re-sending the list a
client already has is not a change.

**Called with a scope-narrowed OAuth token**, the client as it will exist
after the update must be one that token could itself hold — the same rule
as create, judged on the stored `allowed_scopes` when the body omits them.
Otherwise the call returns `403 privilege_escalation` and nothing changes.

403.description:
`privilege_escalation` — the calling OAuth token is scope-narrowed and the
client would exceed its grant after this update. Also returned as ordinary
`forbidden` when the caller lacks `oauth_client:update` (or, for
`step_up_scopes`, `oauth_client:step_up_manage`).

post.description:
Generates a new `client_secret` for a confidential client, immediately
invalidating the old one. **The new secret is shown exactly once.**
Public clients return `400` (they have no secret).

**Rotation is containment.** Every access and refresh token the old
secret minted is revoked in the same transaction as the re-key, so
`/oauth/introspect` reports them inactive immediately rather than for
the remainder of their TTL. If the revocation cannot complete, the
rotation is refused and the old secret keeps working — you never end up
holding a new secret for a client whose old tokens are still live. The
number of tokens revoked is recorded on the audit entry.

**Requires an explicit `oauth_client:rotate_secret` policy grant.** No
seeded role carries it, and a wildcard (`*:*`) rule does not satisfy it.
The `/admin` twin of this operation demands a fresh human step-up
verification, and a machine credential has no session to step up, so the
machine-plane equivalent is a grant the tenant authors deliberately in
Settings -> Permissions. Without it the call returns `403 forbidden` and
no secret is minted. `oauth_client:rotate` alone is not sufficient.

**Called with a scope-narrowed OAuth token**, rotation is refused with
`403 privilege_escalation` unless the client is one that token could itself
hold (the create rule, judged on the stored client) — otherwise it would
hand back the secret of a credential wider than the token.

post.description:
Registers a new BYO server agent and returns its `agent_secret` —
**shown exactly once**; the agent uses it to authenticate its
sessions. Requires a Pro plan or higher; maximum 10 active agents per
data space (Live and Test are counted separately). The agent is
created in the data space of the key that calls this: a `tk_test_` key
on the sandbox host registers a Test agent, whose session bundle
resolves to Test routes and Test secrets only.

**Requires an explicit `agent:create` policy grant.** A wildcard
(`*:*`) rule does not satisfy it — including the `legacy_admin` policy
that every key created before 2026-06-30 still carries. The seeded key
roles that name the action literally (Key - Infrastructure, Key -
Editor) are unaffected and keep working. Without the grant the call
returns `403 forbidden` and no agent is created.

An `agent_secret` is the largest single reveal in the API: it redeems
at `POST /agent/v1/session` for every secret in the data space,
decrypted. Every successful call therefore also emails the account's
owners, out of band.

**A scope-narrowed OAuth token cannot register an agent** and gets
`403 privilege_escalation`: an agent credential authenticates intercepted
requests on the data plane without consulting any scope, so it would exceed
the token's own grant. Register agents with an API key, or with an OAuth
token whose scope is not narrowed.

patch.description:
Sets the per-key destroy safety latch, `deletion_allowed`.

A key version can only be destroyed while this is `true`, so a
cryptographic erasure — which nothing can undo — is never one call
away. Every new key is created with it `false`. The recommended
sequence is: raise the latch, destroy the version, lower it again.

Each change writes a `transit.key.deletion_allowed` audit row
recording the previous and the new value.

deletion_allowed.description: Whether `DELETE /crypto/keys/{name}/versions/{version}` is permitted on this key. Must be a boolean — a string is rejected with a 400 rather than coerced.

post.description: Mints a new key version. New encryptions use the new version; old ciphertexts stay decryptable until their version is destroyed.

delete.description:
Cryptographically erases one key version. Ciphertexts produced with
that version become permanently undecryptable.

Two preconditions, each refused with a **409** carrying a machine-
readable `error.type`:

- `deletion_not_allowed` — the parent key's `deletion_allowed` latch is
  `false`. Raise it with `PATCH /crypto/keys/{name}`, destroy, then
  lower it again.
- `active_version` — the version named is the key's current active
  version. Rotate the key first.

Neither is a server fault, so neither should be retried unchanged.

200.description: Version destroyed. `destroyed` echoes the version number.

409.description: A destroy precondition is not met. `error.type` is `deletion_not_allowed` (raise the key's `deletion_allowed` latch first) or `active_version` (rotate the key first).

error.message: Destroy is not allowed on key 'customer-pii'. Set deletion_allowed = true on the key first (PATCH /v1/crypto/keys/customer-pii), destroy the version, then set it back to false.

post.description:
Mints a single-use capability token (`kct_` prefix). Your backend
(API-key authenticated) mints the token and hands it to the browser;
the browser exchanges it exactly once. The minting key must itself
hold the permission being delegated.

There are TWO kinds of binding, chosen by `action`:

* `decrypt` / `detokenize` are **payload-pinned** — bound to the exact
  `kc:` ciphertext or vault token in `data`, and consumed at
  `POST /client/decrypt` / `POST /client/detokenize`.
* `tokenize` is **vault + origin bound** — the value does not exist
  yet, so there is no payload to pin. Supply `vault` and `origins`
  instead (and no `data`); the token is consumed at
  `POST /client/tokenize`, which requires an `Origin` header matching
  one of them.

vault.description: `tokenize` only, and required for it: the vault (name or id) the browser may write into. Resolved against your tenant and the current Live/Test space; the token stores the resolved id, so renaming the vault does not re-point an outstanding capability.

post.summary: Tokenize from the browser with a capability token
post.description:
Exchanges a single-use `kct_` capability token minted with
`action: tokenize` for a vault token, putting a sensitive value INTO
the bound vault without it ever reaching your own servers.
**Authenticated by the capability token itself**
(`Authorization: Bearer kct_...`), not an API key.

**Browser-only.** This is the one `/v1` endpoint that answers CORS, and
the one that REQUIRES an `Origin` header: the request must come from an
origin bound into the token at mint time, and a request with no
`Origin` is refused with `origin_required` (`403`). Server-side callers
should use `POST /vaults/{vault}/tokens` with an API key instead.

**Two browser callers, and their `Origin` headers mean different
things.** A browser stamps `Origin` with the origin of the DOCUMENT that
issued the request. `KnoxClient.tokenize()` runs on the merchant's own
page, so its `Origin` IS the bound page origin. A KnoxCall hosted field
(`<SecureField>` / `mountSecureField`) runs inside a document served on
`elements.knoxcall.com`, so its `Origin` is the hosted-fields origin —
and it declares the page that framed it in `X-Knox-Page-Origin`, which
is what the binding is then checked against. That header is read ONLY
when `Origin` is this deployment's own hosted-fields origin; from any
other caller it is ignored entirely, so it cannot be used to nominate
someone else's origin.

**CORS.** The `OPTIONS` preflight is answered for any origin with
`Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, authorization,
x-knox-page-origin` and `Vary: Origin`, and grants nothing (credentials
are never allowed). The actual `POST` reflects
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on a successful exchange from a bound
origin, and on **every** response — including refusals — when the
requester is the hosted-fields origin itself, so the field can read the
error code rather than seeing an opaque network failure. A refusal to a
merchant origin omits the header entirely, so a page on an unbound
origin cannot read the response.

**Refusals are uniform.** An unknown, expired, already-spent,
wrong-action, wrong-mode or unbound-origin token all return the same
`401 invalid_token`. A capability token is a bearer secret whose holder
may be an attacker, so the refusal deliberately does not say which
check failed.

counted in `total`; its history remains in the audit log. This matches
the **Live leases** panel in the admin UI.

consecutive failures, so nothing is refreshing or expiring that lease
and its database user is probably still live. It is also exactly the
set counted by the `409 … has N active credential lease(s)` returned
when you delete a connection or a role, so anything blocking a delete
is listed here and can be revoked.

connection and role the lease was minted from, so a lease whose role
row has since been removed returns `role_name: null`.

pagination and returns the pagination fields **inside** `data`.

Creates a tokenization vault with its own encryption key.
`token_format` selects the token shape: `generic` (`tok_` Crockford
base32), or the format-preserving `pan`, `ssn`, `email` formats
(paid plans). Dual-custody vaults support only `generic`.

**A `pan` vault requires a non-empty `allowed_destinations` list.** Card
numbers may only be sent to processors you have named, and are never
returned in the clear: `GET /vaults/{nameOrId}/tokens/{idOrToken}` and
`POST /client/detokenize` both answer `403 vault_destination_refused` for
a `pan` vault. Reference the token from `POST /proxy` (or a Route)
instead, and the value is substituted on the wire.

A value that looks like a payment card number — 13-19 digits after
stripping spaces and hyphens, and Luhn-valid — is refused by every
`token_format` except `pan`.

Payment Required — this action exceeds your plan's limits. Format-preserving
token formats (and other gated features) require a paid plan, or a resource
quota was reached. `error.type: plan_limit`.

`403 vault_destination_refused`, and so does `POST /client/detokenize`.
Reference the token from `POST /proxy` (or a Route) and the value is

For any vault, a token whose `expires_at` has passed answers `404` —

Suggestions to turn detected outbound API usage into a durable route,
from two sources: `agent_monitor` (the install-agent saw a credential on
your servers) and `gateway_traffic` (repeated Ephemeral Proxy calls to a
provider host). Reading this endpoint refreshes gateway-traffic detection
for the current space, then lists both sources. Host-only: evidence never
contains request paths, bodies, or credentials.

post.summary: Promote an opportunity to a route
post.description:
Create a durable route + secret binding from a gateway-traffic
suggestion, in one transaction. The secret bound is either the one you
name, or — for one-click — an escrowed wrap credential pinned to the
host (see POST /wrap/credentials). If neither exists, `400` asks you to
escrow one or pass a secret.

collection_name.description: Collection to file the route under (default "Wrapped APIs").

environment.description: Environment for the route config (default the tenant default).

secret.description: Secret name/id to bind (else an escrowed wrap credential for the host is auto-bound).

200.description: The route was created and the opportunity marked onboarded.

post.description:
Move a third-party provider key (e.g. a Stripe `sk_live_…`) into KnoxCall
custody so it leaves your codebase. The key is stored envelope-encrypted
(BYOK / rotation apply) and bound to `allowed_hosts`. Afterwards the
wrapped SDK sends `X-Knox-Upstream-Auth-Secret: <name>` on `/proxy`
instead of the key, and KnoxCall injects it as the upstream `Authorization`
header **only** for a request whose host is in `allowed_hosts` — the
anti-exfiltration pin.

The value is accepted once and is never returned by any endpoint.

provider.description: Free-form provider label ('stripe', 'openai', …). Not a security boundary.

name.description: Secret name the escrowed key is stored + referenced under.

value.description: The raw provider credential. Sent once; never returned.

hosts.description: The only upstream DNS hostnames this credential may be injected toward (no scheme/port/path/IP literal).

200.description: The credential was escrowed. The value is never echoed.

post.description:
For third-party SDKs that expose ONLY a base-URL override and no
`fetch`/HTTP-client hook. Mints a signed **wrap-token** bound to an
already-escrowed credential (see POST /wrap/credentials) and one upstream
host, and returns a `base_url` to set as the wrapped SDK's base URL.

The SDK then talks to `<base_url>/<its-own-path>`; KnoxCall reconstructs
the real destination, injects the escrowed secret (host-pinned), and
forwards it through the same proxy controls as `/proxy` (SSRF pin, PAN
refusal, plan/rate metering, audit). **Escrow-only** — the SDK's own key
becomes a placeholder; the real key never enters your process.

The wrap-token is a bearer credential embedded in `base_url`; treat it as
a secret. Each token is individually revocable via `DELETE /wrap/tokens/{id}`
(or by deleting the escrowed secret). Only its sha256 is stored server-side.

Needs `secret:read` on the credential. A token issued to a person
(`knoxcall login`, a device or authorization-code grant) also needs
`secret:update` on it: minting a new bearer for a live key is an edit.

secret.description: The escrowed credential (name or id) to inject.

host.description: Upstream host to pin. Optional when the credential allows exactly one host; must be one of its allowed_hosts otherwise.

ttl_seconds.description: Optional token TTL in seconds. Omit for a non-expiring token.

label.description: Optional human label for the token list.

style.description: Which base_url form to return. `path` (`…/wg/<token>/<host>`) is always available. `subdomain` (`<label>.wrap.knoxcall.com`) is only available when the operator has enabled the wildcard-subdomain gateway; a `400` is returned otherwise. Omitted ⇒ `subdomain` when enabled, else `path`. NOTE: the subdomain label travels in the TLS SNI (plaintext on the wire) — weaker token confidentiality than the path form; prefer a short `ttl_seconds`.

200.description: A gateway token + base_url was minted.

id.description: Token id — pass to DELETE /wrap/tokens/{id} to revoke.

token.description: Bearer credential; also embedded in the path base_url. Treat as secret.

base_url.description: Set this as the wrapped SDK's base URL.

get.description: List this space's gateway tokens (metadata only — the token itself is never stored or returned).

get.summary: Which hosts an intercept-enabled Route covers
get.description:
The manifest every KnoxCall SDK's transparent interceptor polls: for
this space and ONE environment, the upstream hosts that an enabled Route
with `intercept_enabled` on covers, and the slug to send them under
(`x-knoxcall-route`). A third-party SDK's call to a listed host is sent
through that Route (the Route injects the stored secret); a listed host
with no Route is sent through the ephemeral proxy; everything else is
untouched. Routes targeting KnoxCall's own hosts are never listed.

`version` is a content hash of the entries and doubles as the `ETag`;
send it back as `If-None-Match` and a steady-state poll answers `304`
with no body. Poll at `ttl_seconds`.

Scope: `routes:read` — this lists which routes exist, which is a routes
read; it grants nothing a `GET /routes` caller does not already see.

parameters.name: environment
parameters.description: The environment to resolve for. Omitted ⇒ the tenant's default environment, exactly as a data-plane call with no `x-knoxcall-environment` header resolves. A name that does not exist in this space answers `400`.

parameters.name: If-None-Match
parameters.description: The `ETag` from a previous response; a match answers `304`.

200.description: The manifest for this space and environment.

304.description: Unchanged since the `If-None-Match` version; no body.

post.summary: Report uncovered egress the SDK's interceptor saw
post.description:
The complement of the intercept manifest. Every KnoxCall SDK's
transparent interceptor sees every outbound request its process makes;
the ones that carried a credential but were NOT intercepted — no Route
covers the host, or a Route exists with interception off — are reported
here so the dashboard's **Uncovered egress** page can show which hosts
still have credentials leaving the process, and which existing Route
would cover each one.

Reporting is **on by default** in every SDK's `intercept()` and is
switched off per install with `observe_uncovered: false` (or, per
process, `KNOXCALL_OBSERVE_UNCOVERED=off`). What is sent is metadata
only: the host, the first path segment (`/` or `/<one segment>`), the
method, the **name** of the header the credential travelled in, and
counts with first/last-seen timestamps. Credential values, full paths,
query strings, bodies and client addresses are never captured, and the
server refuses an entry that carries anything else in those fields.

Semantics: at most 200 observations per request (`413` beyond). Each
entry is validated on its own — a bad entry is **dropped and counted**
under a reason, never a `400` for the batch. Accepted entries are
merged per (host, first_segment, method, header_name, UTC day of
`last_seen`): counts add, timestamps merge as min/max. A space may add
at most 5,000 distinct keys per day; beyond that entries are dropped
under `daily_cap`. Rows are kept for 30 days. `sandbox` is taken from
the reporting credential's mode.

Scope: `routes:read` — exactly the manifest's gate. Policy: `route:read`
on `*`, evaluated before the body is read, so an ungranted credential
gets `403` whatever it sends.
A token issued to a person (`knoxcall login`, a device or
authorization-code grant) also needs `route:create`, checked at the same
point.

202.description: The batch was processed. `accepted + dropped` equals the number of observations sent; `reasons` says why each dropped entry was refused.

413.description: More than 200 observations in one request. Split the batch.

delete.description:
Revoke a single gateway token by id (from the mint response or the list).
Immediately invalidates it for all future `/wg` requests. An already-revoked
or unknown id in this space is a 404.
Needs `secret:read`; a token issued to a person also needs `secret:update`.

/proxy.description:
One-shot proxy: forward a request to any HTTPS upstream while KnoxCall
resolves `{{ token: ... }}` template expressions (vault tokens) in the
body, query string, and forwarded headers on the wire. Accepts any HTTP
method — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE all behave identically apart
from the forwarded method.

**Request headers:**
- `X-Knox-Proxy-URL` (required) — the upstream URL. Must be `https://`
  with a DNS hostname (IP literals are rejected).
- `X-Knox-Timeout-Ms` (optional) — upstream timeout, capped at 30000
  (default 25000).
- `X-Knox-Encrypted` (optional) — base64-encoded JSON body (v1 scope;
  not real JWE).
- `X-Knox-Proxy-Mode: transparent` (optional) — forward the request body
  and `Content-Type` byte-verbatim and skip `{{ token }}` templating. Use
  this to proxy a third-party SDK's own request format (e.g. Stripe's
  `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`). Omit for the default JSON +
  template behaviour.
- `X-Knox-Upstream-Authorization` (optional) — value mapped to the
  UPSTREAM `Authorization` header (the provider's own credential). Never
  logged or stored; distinct from the KnoxCall API credential that
  authenticates the proxy call itself. Validated as a single line of
  printable characters (≤ 8192 bytes).
- `X-Knox-Upstream-Auth-Secret` (optional) — the NAME of an escrowed wrap
  credential (see POST /wrap/credentials). KnoxCall resolves + decrypts it
  and injects it as the upstream `Authorization` header, but only if the
  upstream host is in the credential's `allowed_hosts` (else `403
  wrap_host_not_allowed`). Mutually exclusive with
  `X-Knox-Upstream-Authorization`.
- `X-Knox-Upstream-Auth-Scheme` (optional) — auth scheme for the resolved
  secret (default `Bearer`; `none` injects the raw value).

All other headers are forwarded to the upstream except hop-by-hop
headers, the reserved `x-knox-*` / `authorization` / `host` /
`content-length` headers, `cookie` (your browser's KnoxCall session is
never forwarded), the control headers KnoxCall reads itself
(`x-knoxcall-key`, `x-knoxcall-route`, `x-knoxcall-environment`,
`x-knoxcall-signature`, `x-knoxcall-agent-id`, `x-knoxcall-agent-token`,
`x-knoxcall-client-assertion`, `x-knoxcall-origin` and `x-knoxcall-env`),
the headers a reverse proxy adds to describe the connection to KnoxCall
rather than your request (`x-forwarded-for`, `x-forwarded-host`,
`x-forwarded-proto`, `x-forwarded-server`, `x-real-ip`, `true-client-ip`,
`x-client-cert-verify`, `x-client-cert-thumbprint` and
`x-client-cert-subject`), the request headers Cloudflare adds
(`cf-connecting-ip`, `cf-ray`, `cf-ipcountry` and the rest of the exact
names listed at
https://docs.knoxcall.com/api-reference/request-headers), and `x-api-key`
WHEN its value is a KnoxCall credential
(`tk_`, `kc_`, `kr_` or `AKE…`) — that is the key you authenticated with,
and it is not for your upstream. An `x-api-key` holding your upstream's
own key (`sk-ant-…`, and so on) is forwarded unchanged.

Every name above is matched exactly, in any letter case; apart from
`x-knox-` there is no prefix rule. A header that only resembles one of
them is forwarded, including the `cf-access-client-id` /
`cf-access-client-secret` / `cf-access-token` credentials for an upstream
of yours that sits behind Cloudflare Access.

**Response:** a passthrough of the upstream's status, headers (minus
hop-by-hop), and body — not the KnoxCall JSON envelope.

Every response also carries the **KnoxCall response block**: the `X-Knox-*`
headers that describe KnoxCall's own half of the call, distinct from
anything your upstream sent. The whole `x-knox-` response namespace is
reserved — an upstream header in it is dropped, never relayed — so these
values are always KnoxCall speaking.

| header | meaning |
|---|---|
| `X-Knox-Request-Id` | the call id; quote it to support |
| `X-Knox-Origin` | `upstream` or `knoxcall` — who produced this status and body |
| `X-Knox-Upstream-Status` | the status your upstream returned. **Present only on a genuine forward** |
| `X-Knox-Error` | KnoxCall's error code, on a KnoxCall-originated refusal |
| `X-Knox-Latency-Ms` | total time inside KnoxCall, in milliseconds |
| `X-Knox-Latency-Phase` | `complete`, or `first-byte` on a streamed response |
| `X-Knox-Upstream-Ms` / `X-Knox-Overhead-Ms` | the split: time in your provider vs time in KnoxCall. Omitted when unmeasured |
| `X-Knox-Sandbox` | whether the call ran in the Test data space |
| `X-Knox-RateLimit-Route` / `-Tenant` / `-Monthly` | `limit=…, remaining=…, reset=…` per limiter |
| `Server-Timing` | `knoxcall;dur=…, knoxcall_upstream;dur=…`, appended to any your upstream sent |

**To tell a KnoxCall error from a provider error, branch on the ABSENCE of
`X-Knox-Upstream-Status`.** It is present if and only if a real upstream
response was received, so "no `X-Knox-Upstream-Status`" means the gateway
answered and the call never reached your provider — the check a wrapped
SDK needs so it does not retry a KnoxCall 429 against a provider limit
that is not the one refusing it. A KnoxCall-originated refusal (plan gate,
validation, SSRF/PAN refusal, upstream failure) additionally carries
`X-Knox-Error` and repeats the whole block as a `knoxcall` object beside
`error` in the JSON body. `X-Knox-Destination-Status` is the older spelling
of `X-Knox-Upstream-Status` and is still sent. When a durable route now covers the
upstream host (you promoted this traffic — see POST /opportunities/{id}/accept),
the response also carries `X-Knox-Promoted-Route: <slug>` so a wrapper can
switch off the ephemeral path.

**PCI:** requests to known raw-card endpoints (`api.stripe.com/v1/tokens`,
`/v1/sources`) are refused with `403 pan_endpoint_refused` — tokenize card
data with a KnoxCall vault or `@knoxcall/browser` and send the token.

**Test-mode test cards.** In the Test data space four documented card
numbers behave in documented ways so a failure path can be exercised
without a processor account. `4242 4242 4242 4242` forwards normally;
`4000 0000 0000 0002` is NOT forwarded and answers `402
sandbox_test_card_declined`; `4000 0000 0000 3220` is NOT forwarded and
answers `402 sandbox_test_card_requires_action`; `4000 0000 0000 0069`
forwards but tokenizes with a past `card_expires_on`. Both refusals are
KnoxCall's own simulated outcome and not any processor's — nothing is sent
upstream — and both are recognised ONLY for a value a `pan` vault
RELEASED, never for a card number in your own request body (that is still
`403`). In the Live data space all four are ordinary card numbers. See
/essentials/vaults/overview#test-cards.

**Responses are re-tokenized when a card number was detokenized.** If the
request resolved a `{{ token: ... }}` from a `pan`-format vault, the
upstream's reply is scanned for that exact number — however the upstream
spaced it — and each occurrence is replaced with the token before the
response reaches you, in the body (JSON at any depth, form-encoded, text)
and in header values such as `Location`. Only the values THIS request
opened, and only `pan` vaults: a different card number the upstream
mentions, and any `generic`/`ssn`/`email` value, are untouched. Two
consequences: KnoxCall sends `Accept-Encoding: identity` upstream on such a
request and WITHHOLDS the reply with `502 response_not_retokenizable` if it
comes back compressed or binary (it cannot be scanned, and an unscanned
reply is not forwarded); and a request that both detokenizes a `pan` token
and asks for a streamed response is refused with
`409 pan_streaming_unsupported`, because a card number can straddle any
chunk boundary the upstream picks. Each re-tokenized response writes a
`vault.retokenize` audit entry with the vault id and the occurrence count —
never the number, never the token.

**Scope: `proxy:invoke`, on every method.** If the access token you call
with was deliberately narrowed, its grant must include `proxy:invoke` (or
`proxy:*`); `proxy:read` and `proxy:write` are refused with `403
insufficient_scope`. Calling the proxy is not a read of a resource and not
a write to one — it resolves and decrypts an escrowed credential and spends
it against the upstream you name — and because one handler serves every
verb, a bodyless `GET` does exactly what a `POST` does. This mirrors
`routes:invoke` on the route-configured data plane. An un-narrowed token
(and a raw API key) is unaffected.

Firewall policies are tenant-scoped and shared across gateways: one policy can be
attached to any number of agents (`firewall_policy_id`) and MCP servers. Policies are
versioned by name — creating under an existing name returns a new version, and agents
stay bound to the version id they reference.

post.description:
Creates a policy. Every `kind: regex` rule is compiled server-side with the same
linear-time engine the data plane runs, so a pattern that cannot execute is rejected
here (400 `unsafe_regex`) rather than stored and silently skipped at scan time.
Lookahead, lookbehind and backreferences are not supported.

`action` decides what a match does: `warn` (record, allow), `tag` (mark, allow) or
`block` (refuse the request with HTTP 400 `firewall_block`). An agent with no policy
attached still runs the built-in prompt-injection patterns but can never exceed `warn`.

post.summary: Dry-run firewall rules against sample text
post.description:
Runs the built-in prompt-injection patterns plus the supplied rules over `text` and
returns every match, without saving anything. Rules are compiled first, so this
endpoint refuses exactly what create/update refuse — a pattern that passes here is one
that will actually run in the data plane.

heuristics.description: Candidate rules to test alongside the built-ins.

patch.description: Updates the policy in place (the version is not bumped). Rules are re-validated.

delete.description:
Refused with 409 `policy_in_use` while any agent or MCP server is still attached — the
foreign keys are `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so an unchecked delete would silently detach
every consumer and downgrade an enforcing `block` policy to no policy at all.

get.description:
A PII policy is a named bundle of recognizer ids plus a `default_action`. Policies are
tenant-scoped and shared across gateways.

An EMPTY `recognizer_ids` does not mean "no recognizers" — it means "every enabled
recognizer this tenant owns".

post.description:
Every id in `recognizer_ids` must be a recognizer this tenant owns. A foreign or
unknown id is refused with 400 `recognizer_not_found` rather than stored: the column
has no foreign key, and the data-plane loader intersects with the recognizer row's own
tenant, so a stored foreign id resolves to nothing — a policy that lists three
recognizers and runs zero, indistinguishable from working redaction until the PII
reaches the provider.

Custom PII policies are a Pro entitlement; a tenant who already owns one keeps
authoring (402 `plan_limit` otherwise).

patch.description:
Updates in place (the version is not bumped). `recognizer_ids` is re-validated against
the tenant's own recognizers. Passing `[]` resets the policy to "every enabled
recognizer" — that is a widening, not a clearing.

delete.description:
Refused with 409 `policy_in_use` while any agent still references the policy. The
foreign key is `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so an unchecked delete would detach every bound
agent and turn redaction OFF for each of them with no error and no signal.

get.description:
A recognizer is one tenant-defined detector — an internal employee-id shape, a
customer-reference format, anything the built-in entity tier does not know about.

post.description:
A `kind: regex` pattern is compiled server-side with the same linear-time engine the
data plane runs, so lookahead, lookbehind and backreferences are refused here (400
`invalid_regex` / `unsafe_regex`) rather than stored and silently skipped at scan time —
a skipped detector is a fail-OPEN.

A `whitelist` recognizer is ordered ahead of every other detector, so a pattern that
matches arbitrary text is refused: one such row would suppress the whole built-in tier.

post.summary: Dry-run a recognizer pattern against sample text
post.description:
Compiles the candidate pattern and runs it over `text`, saving nothing. It uses the
SAME compiler and the SAME detector builder as the write path and the data plane, so a
pattern that passes here is one that will actually execute.

Do not preview locally: a client-side regex engine accepts lookahead, lookbehind and
backreferences that the server refuses, so a local preview shows matches for a
recognizer that can never run and then 400s on save.

patch.description:
The MERGED state is validated, not the patch: `pattern`, `kind` and `action` together
decide whether a pattern is compiled and how the detector is ranked, so a patch
carrying only one of them is re-checked against the stored values.

delete.description:
Refused with 409 `recognizer_in_use` while any PII policy still lists it. Silently
removing the id would not shrink the policy: an EMPTY `recognizer_ids` means "every
enabled recognizer", so dropping the last id would WIDEN it. Remove the recognizer
from each policy first.

post.summary: Exchange a CI OIDC token for an AI-gateway capability token
post.description:
RFC 8693 token exchange. Trade a workload identity token your CI provider already
mints — GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, or any OIDC issuer you have registered
a binding for — for a short-lived KnoxCall capability token. **No KnoxCall
credential is stored in your CI system**: the subject token is the credential, and
it is verified against the issuer's published JWKS.

**The host is the tenant data plane**, not `api.knoxcall.com` — the same subdomain
your agent URLs and MCP connect URLs use. `/v1/ai/`, `/v1/mcp/` and `/v1/oauth/`
are handed to the proxy router only on a tenant data-plane host. Sending this
request to `api.knoxcall.com` answers **401**, which reads like a rejected
`subject_token` but means the endpoint is not served there.

This endpoint is NOT the tenant OAuth 2.1 token endpoint. That one is
`POST https://api.knoxcall.com/oauth/token` on the root host, mints `kc_` management
tokens, and takes `client_credentials` / `authorization_code` / `refresh_token` /
`device_code`. This one lives under `/v1` on the tenant host, takes only
`urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange`, and mints an AI-gateway phantom
token for the data plane (`POST /v1/ai/...`, or `/v1/mcp/<slug>` when `resource` is
supplied). Sending a request for one to the other is an
`unsupported_grant_type`.

**Unauthenticated by design.** The subject token IS the credential. It must be a
JWS-compact `id_token` signed by a registered issuer, unexpired, and satisfy the
binding's attribute conditions (repository, ref, workflow, …).

**`resource` narrows the token to `tool` kind.** Supplying an RFC 8707 `resource` —
the `resource` value from an MCP server's create/get response — binds that MCP
resource into the capability HMAC, so the minted token is confined to exactly that
one server and is refused on the `/v1/ai` plane. Omit `resource` and you get an
`agent`-kind token instead, which is refused by `/v1/mcp`. A repeated or array
`resource` is `invalid_target`, never silently dropped: dropping it would mint an
UNCONFINED token while the client believes it is audience-restricted.

The token is returned once and is not retrievable. It appears in
`GET /v1/ai-gateway/gateways/{gatewayId}/tokens` (never its plaintext) and is
revoked with `DELETE /v1/ai-gateway/gateways/{gatewayId}/tokens/{tokenId}` — NOT
the per-agent revoke, because a federated token has no agent.

Accepts `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (RFC 6749) or `application/json`.

or a `resource` that is repeated / not an MCP URI on this origin),

`subject_token`, unmet attribute conditions).

post.summary: Call an AI provider through the gateway
post.description:
Forwards the request to the agent's configured upstream with the tenant's provider
credential injected server-side, after applying every control the agent carries:
the prompt firewall, PII tokenization, the model allow/deny lists, the tool
allowlist, the daily/monthly budget and the token's own signed caps. The response
is screened on the way back (PII redaction, canary detection, output-schema
validation) before it reaches you.

**The body and the response are the PROVIDER's**, not KnoxCall's — this is a
governed proxy, so an existing Anthropic or OpenAI SDK works unchanged once its
base URL is the agent's `agent_url`. The only KnoxCall-shaped body you can receive
here is a refusal (see below).

**Streaming.** Ask the provider to stream — `"stream": true`, or Gemini's
`:streamGenerateContent` endpoint — and, when the agent has `streaming_enabled`,
the response is Server-Sent Events with PII redaction applied mid-stream. An
`Accept: text/event-stream` header alone does not stream; the response is served
buffered. Streaming is refused with `400 streaming_redaction_unsupported` on an
endpoint whose event stream KnoxCall cannot redact (for example the OpenAI
Responses API), and with `400 streaming_disabled` when the agent does not stream. A stream that fails after its first frame ends with a
terminal `event: error` frame whose `data` is the same error object documented
below — the status line is already committed by then, so the frame is the only
place the reason can go.

**Every response carries `X-Request-Id`.** Quote it in support requests; it is the
key into the audit trail for that exact call. Refusals additionally write one
`ai_gateway.request_denied` audit row.

scopes.secrets:oauth_token: Retrieve a live upstream OAuth2 access token (GET /v1/secrets/{id}/oauth2/token). Distinct from secrets:read because the call refreshes the credential at the provider.
scopes.vaults:detokenize: Turn a vault token back into its original value. Required by GET /v1/vaults/{vault}/tokens/{token}, by a token template reference in a /v1/proxy body, and by creating a `detokenize` route action. Distinct from vaults:read, which lists vaults and token metadata and never returns a value.
scopes.transit:decrypt: Open a portable `kc:` ciphertext with a tenant transit key. Required by creating a `decrypt` route action, which stores a standing instruction to open every matching field on every later request through that route. It is the same capability name the policy engine uses for POST /v1/decrypt. No routes scope satisfies it — managing a route is not permission to open the data flowing through it.
scopes.proxy:invoke: Call the one-shot ephemeral proxy (any method on /v1/proxy). Required for EVERY verb — the proxy is one capability behind one handler, and a bodyless GET spends an escrowed credential exactly as a POST does. Neither proxy:read nor proxy:write satisfies it.

scopes.secrets:read: Read secret metadata. Does NOT include retrieving a live OAuth2 access token.
scopes.secrets:oauth_token: Retrieve a live upstream OAuth2 access token (GET /v1/secrets/{id}/oauth2/token). Distinct from secrets:read because the call refreshes the credential at the provider.
